title: Counting to 1000 in Grade 2: Skip-Counting, Compare & Order + Free Quiz
meta_desc: A Grade 2 guide to counting to 1000: skip-count in 2s, 5s, 10s and 100s, count on and back, and compare numbers to 999, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Skip-counting is not busywork — it is the runway to multiplication. Here is how I take a Grade 2 child from counting on by ones all the way to comparing numbers up to 999, with a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Grade 2 child to count from 397 and watch what happens at 399. Most pause, then say ‘three hundred and one hundred’ or freeze completely, because crossing a hundred feels like a cliff. Counting to 1000 in Grade 2 is really about turning those cliffs into small, boring steps — and about learning to jump in 2s, 5s, 10s and 100s instead of trudging one at a time. Get this right and multiplication next year arrives half-taught already.

I teach it in a fixed order: count on and back by ones first, then skip-count, then before/after/between, then comparing. Each layer leans on the one under it. Here is the whole path, with the counters and hundred-chart I actually use.

Start where the child is: counting on and back from any number

Before any skip-counting, a child must be able to start from an awkward number — say 268 — and count on: 269, 270, 271. Then count back: 268, 267, 266. The two hard spots are the tens boundary (crossing from 269 to 270) and the hundreds boundary (699 to 700). Drill those two crossings on their own. I keep a printed hundred-chart handy and simply point: ‘What comes after 699?’ Do it for a week and the cliff disappears.

The counting-back blind spot

Almost every child finds counting back harder than counting on, and most Grade 2 practice quietly ignores it. Do not. Counting back from 305 — 304, 303, 302, 301, 300, 299 — is the exact skill that subtraction across a hundred will need in a few months. Ten minutes of backward counting now saves a term of confusion later.

Skip-counting: the runway to multiplication

Skip-counting is counting in equal jumps. Count in 2s and you get 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Count in 5s and you get 5, 10, 15, 20. Here is the part parents miss: 5, 10, 15, 20 is the five times table. A child who can skip-count in 5s to 100 has, without knowing it, learned 5 × 1 up to 5 × 20. When formal multiplication starts in Grade 3, these children are not memorising cold facts; they are naming a pattern they already chant.

Teach the four core jumps in this order — 10s, then 2s, then 5s, then 100s:

  • 10s are easiest because only the tens digit moves: 10, 20, 30… up to 100, then 110, 120.
  • 2s build the idea of even numbers; ask ‘does 2s ever land on 7?’ and let them discover it never does.
  • 5s always end in 5 or 0 — a self-checking rule children love.
  • 100s unlock the whole thousand: 100, 200, 300… 900, 1000. This is where 1000 first shows up as a real, reachable number.

Start the jumps from anywhere, not just zero

Any child can rattle off 10, 20, 30. The real test is skip-counting in 10s from 44: 54, 64, 74. Or in 5s from 30. Starting off-zero is where skip-counting stops being a memorised song and becomes a tool. I push this hard, because it is the single biggest predictor of who finds multiplication easy later.

Before, after and between

Once counting on is smooth, ‘before’ and ‘after’ are quick wins: the number after 549 is 550, the number before 600 is 599. ‘Between’ is the trickier one — what number is between 798 and 800? A surprising number of children guess 801. Slow this down with a number line drawn on paper and let them hop. These three ideas sound trivial, but they are the language every word problem uses, so fluency here pays off constantly.

Comparing and ordering numbers to 999

Comparing two three-digit numbers has one rule worth drilling until it is automatic: look at the hundreds digit first. 512 beats 498 the moment you see 5 against 4 — the other digits do not matter. Only when the hundreds match do you move to the tens, and only then to the ones. I teach the symbols as a hungry mouth that always opens toward the bigger number: 512 > 498, and 340 < 403.

Ordering follows naturally. Give a child four number cards — 207, 720, 270, 702 — and the digits look almost the same, which is exactly the point. Sort by hundreds first (2s before 7s), then break ties. This same left-to-right habit is how they will compare thousands and lakhs later, so it is worth building carefully now.

A quick game that works

Write digits 0–9 on slips in a bowl. Each player draws three and arranges them into the largest number they can. Biggest number wins the round. Children learn place-value comparison faster from three rounds of this than from a page of > and < questions, because they want the bigger number.

A realistic weekly plan

Ten minutes a day, split like this: two days on counting on and back across hundreds, two days on skip-counting starting off-zero, one day on before/after/between, and the weekend on comparing and ordering with the card game. Keep a hundred-chart on the fridge. Do not rush to 1000 in week one — a child who owns counting to 300 in every direction will reach 1000 far more securely than one marched to it in a hurry.

Test what your child can do

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly these skills — skip-counting, counting back, before and after, and comparing numbers to 999. Let your child try it, then talk through the explanations for anything they miss. When they are ready for written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded counting questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Counting to 1000 Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on skip-counting, counting back, before and after, and comparing numbers. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Counting in 5s adds five each time, and the number always ends in 5 or 0. After 25 comes 30.
Counting on by one across a hundreds boundary: after 699 comes 700.

questions.q: Count back by ones from 302: 302, 301, ___. What is next?
questions.explanation: Counting back means one less each time: 302, 301, 300. Next would be 300.
In 100s only the hundreds digit changes, adding one hundred each time. After 600 comes 700.
The number line goes 798, 799, 800. So 799 sits between them.
Compare the hundreds digit first: 5 is more than 4, so 512 is greater than 498.
Counting in 10s adds ten each time, so only the tens digit moves: 44, 54, 64, 74.

questions.q: Put in order from smallest to largest: 270, 207, 702. Which is smallest?
questions.explanation: Look at the hundreds digit first: 207 and 270 both have 2 hundreds, 702 has 7. Between 207 and 270, the tens digit 0 is less than 7, so 207 is smallest.

faq.q: Why is skip-counting so important in Grade 2?
faq.a: It is the bridge to multiplication. Counting in 5s to 100 is the five times table in disguise, so a child who skip-counts fluently meets multiplication in Grade 3 already half-prepared.

faq.q: My child can count to 1000 but stumbles at 199 and 299. Is that normal?
faq.a: Completely normal. Crossing a hundreds boundary is the hardest part of counting to 1000. Practise just those crossings — 199 to 200, 299 to 300 — on their own for a week and it settles.

faq.q: Should I teach counting back as well as counting on?
faq.a: Yes, and most parents skip it. Counting back from any number is the exact skill subtraction across a hundred will need soon, so give it equal time now.

faq.q: What is the quickest way to teach comparing three-digit numbers?
faq.a: One rule: check the hundreds digit first, and only move to the tens when the hundreds are equal. Drill that left-to-right habit and comparing becomes automatic.
